rows: View of Angoulême

Paul Michel Hossard was an amateur who loved making daguerreotypes of buildings in his French hometown. This view of Angoulême shows the town on its hill as people saw it in the first years of photography.
What do you see on the hilltop?
Man with Cat
This is one of the earliest photographs of a cat known to exist. A man sits for a daguerreotype around 1840 with his cat, and both had to stay still for several seconds.
Is the cat holding still? What would you do if you were the cat?
Lace

William Henry Fox Talbot laid a piece of lace on light-sensitive paper in 1841 and let the sun print it. The delicate threads show every hole and loop, and Talbot said it showed how photography could copy anything.
Look at the pattern. Can you find a shape that repeats?
Country House
Hippolyte Bayard photographed a country house in France in 1842. He took many views around Paris, and the plain buildings show how ordinary life looked in the 1840s.
How many windows can you count?
Rooftops of Paris
Hippolyte Bayard photographed the roofs of Paris from a high window in 1842. Rooftop views were popular with early photographers because they could set up in a quiet spot.
How many chimneys can you find?
The Attic
Bayard photographed the inside of an attic with tools and old things stacked about. Looking at humble places like this was rare for the time.
What would you find in an old attic?
James Linton and Three Boys, Newhaven
Hill and Adamson photographed a fisherman with three boys in the Scottish fishing village of Newhaven. They made hundreds of these everyday pictures, which look like quiet paintings.
What do the boys' clothes tell you about their lives?
Newhaven Fishermen
Three fishermen from Newhaven pose in a group, photographed by David Octavius Hill. His partner Robert Adamson built the cameras and made the paper negatives.
Which of the three looks most relaxed?
The Ladder
Talbot photographed a ladder leaning against a house with people at the windows. He chose a plain subject on purpose, to show that photography could capture a moment from everyday life.
How many people can you find?
Jeremiah Clemens
Jeremiah Clemens was a senator from Alabama who also wrote novels. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1840s, when senators had to travel to a studio to be photographed.
Does he look like a writer or a senator?
The Cloisters of Lacock Abbey
Talbot photographed the covered walkways of his old family home, Lacock Abbey, for his book The Pencil of Nature. It was the first book published with real photographs pasted in.
How do the arches lead your eye along the walkway?
The Fruit Sellers
Talbot photographed fruit sellers with baskets and a cart. He printed it as a calotype, a paper negative, so he could make as many copies as he liked.
What fruit might they be selling?
Henry Inman
Henry Inman was a well-known American painter, and Brady photographed him in the 1840s. Photography was beginning to compete with painted portraits, and many painters were curious about it.
Why might a painter be curious about the camera?
High Street, Oxford
Talbot photographed High Street in Oxford, England, in about 1840. The street looks nearly the same today, which is one reason early photographs make good time machines.
What buildings would you still see in Oxford today?
Pliny Earle
Pliny Earle was a doctor who studied mental illness and wrote about it. Brady photographed many scientists, writers and doctors for his gallery of notable Americans.
What would you ask a doctor from 1844?
Articles of Porcelain
Talbot photographed shelves of china to show that the camera could record fine detail. The cups and plates stand like little characters, and the picture helped sell his invention.
Which piece of china do you like best?
John Davis
John Davis was a governor of Massachusetts and a U.S. senator. Mathew Brady photographed him in his studio, where politicians liked to sit for a daguerreotype.
What do you think a governor wanted to look like?
A Fruit Piece
This still life from Talbot's The Pencil of Nature shows fruit and a plate on a table. He wrote that the camera could make pictures that painters make, only faster.
What fruit do you see?
Mill at Saint-Ouen
Bayard photographed a mill beside a river near Paris in 1845. Mills made lovely early subjects because their shapes and shadows are strong.
Where do you think the water goes?
Arch in a Farmyard, Swansea
Calvert Richard Jones was a clergyman, mathematician and musician who made daguerreotypes. He photographed an old stone arch standing in a farmyard in Wales.
What do you think the arch was once part of?
Still Life with Statuary and Drapery
Bayard liked to arrange plaster casts of ancient sculptures with cloth and set them in front of his camera. These still lifes were some of the first pictures made to be art, not records.
Why do you think he chose statues?
Medallion Portrait of a Woman
Southworth and Hawes of Boston made daguerreotypes with large plates and soft light. This portrait of a woman sits in a round frame like a coin.
How does the round frame change the way you look at her?
Temple of Athena Nike
A Greek photographer photographed a small temple on the Acropolis in Athens. This is a view of an ancient monument seen through the eyes of someone who lived nearby.
What shapes do the columns make?
Construction Worker, Paris
A construction worker stands in the wooden frame of a building in Paris in 1845. Hippolyte Bayard photographed working people at a time when few photographers did.
What is he building?
Gorge of the Eaux-Chaudes Road
John Stewart photographed the new road through a rocky gorge in the Pyrenees. British tourists came here by carriage in the 1840s.
How would you travel along this road?
View of the Zeil, Frankfurt
Talbot photographed this street from a hotel window in Frankfurt in 1846. Looking out a window was an easy way to photograph with a heavy camera.
What would you see from your window?
Doorway to the Sèvres Factory
Louis-Rémy Robert, who was trained as a painter on porcelain, photographed the doorway of the Sèvres porcelain factory. Photographs of buildings like this are among the first ever.
What do you think was made inside?
Self-Portrait
Louis-Rémy Robert photographed himself on waxed paper negatives he made in the early 1850s. He later worked at the famous Sèvres factory.
What do you see in his expression?
St. Anthony Falls from Across the River

An unknown photographer made an instantaneous daguerreotype of the falls on the Mississippi River in Minnesota in 1848. The falling water looks sharp for a moment, which was a big achievement for the time.
Is the water blurry or sharp? Why is that surprising?
Dolley Madison
Dolley Madison was the wife of the fourth U.S. president, James Madison, and a famous Washington hostess. Mathew Brady photographed her in the late 1840s when she was an old woman.
What do you think she was like?
Fountain of Sophia, Constantinople
Ernest de Caranza was a French engineer in Istanbul who took up photography. He photographed a fountain in a city that was then called Constantinople.
Fountains were places to meet. Where do people meet in your town?
The Temple of Isis at Philae
Maxime Du Camp took this photograph on an island in the Nile in Egypt in 1849. The temple was built over 2,000 years ago, and he was one of the first photographers to show Egypt to the world.
What do the columns and walls look like up close?
Rock-cut Temple, Abu Simbel
Du Camp traveled up the Nile and photographed the giant carved temple at Abu Simbel, which was buried in sand at that time. His pictures made people in France excited about ancient Egypt.
What do you think it was like to find a temple half buried in sand?
Alice Montgomery
A little girl named Alice Montgomery sat for a daguerreotype portrait around 1850. Pictures of children were cherished, because the family could keep a copy forever.
What is she holding or wearing?
Two Children with Toys
Two children pose with their toys in a daguerreotype made around 1850. Children had to sit very still for the exposure, so their toys helped keep them calm.
What toys would you have taken to be photographed?
Child with a Drum
A child holds a toy drum in a daguerreotype made around 1850. The unknown photographer worked hard with a heavy camera to capture a moving child.
What sound would the drum make?
Artist with His Palette and Brushes
An unknown photographer made a personal portrait of a painter holding his tools. The daguerreotype shows how artists and photographers learned from each other.
What do his tools tell you about his job?
The Music Teacher and His Wife
A music teacher and his wife posed for this daguerreotype, which shows how sitters could suggest how they wanted to look. The couple chose to show their love of music.
What instrument do you see?
Mrs. John R. Johnston
John R. Johnston was an artist and musician who also made daguerreotypes. He made a portrait of his wife around 1850.
Why might an artist take so many pictures of his family?
Young Woman in Pantalettes
A young woman poses in pantalettes, the long ruffled underpants that girls wore under their dresses in the 1840s. Daguerreotypes like this one show us what people wore.
What would be hard about wearing this every day?
Monkey on a Branch
Louis Jules Duboscq-Soleil made this stereoscopic picture of a monkey on a branch. Stereoscopes showed two nearly identical pictures that seemed to pop out in 3D, and they were a big craze.
How could two pictures make one 3D picture?
Portrait of a Young Woman
It seemed a miracle that anyone could afford to have an accurate picture of themselves. This young woman sat for a daguerreotype around 1850, which cost much less than a painting.
How would it feel to see yourself in a picture for the first time?
The Great Temple of Isis at Philae
Maxime Du Camp photographed this temple on an island in the Nile. It was later moved to a new island to save it from rising water, so his picture shows its original place.
Why would a temple be moved?
Workman in a Red Flannel Shirt
Daguerreotypes were mostly of wealthy people, but this one shows a laborer in a work shirt and suspenders. It is a rare picture of an ordinary worker around 1850.
What do you think his job was?
Adolescent Wearing Earrings and a Suit
A 12-year-old poses for a daguerreotype in a suit and earrings. Early portraits show how people dressed up and how fashions have changed.
What would you wear for a portrait?
Studying the Face
Guillaume Duchenne photographed an old man whose face muscles he made move with small electric shocks. These photographs were among the first used to study how faces show feelings.
What does his face seem to say?
Allegorical Sculpture of Industry, Pont du Carrousel
Charles Marville photographed a statue of Industry on a Paris bridge. The sculptures were carved in stone, and Marville's picture shows their weight and shadow.
What is the statue holding?
The Taj Mahal
Dr. John Murray photographed the Taj Mahal from the bank of the Yamuna River in the 1850s. It is a very early photograph of a world-famous building, taken by a doctor with a huge camera.
What do you think it was like to carry such a camera in the heat?
Gutenbergplatz, Mainz
Charles Marville photographed this square in Mainz, Germany, named after Johannes Gutenberg, who invented the printing press. It is a nice fit that a photographer visited the town of printing.
Why was printing an important invention?
Reims Cathedral, Central Portal
Marville photographed the doorway of Reims Cathedral in France. Kings of France were crowned there for centuries, and the stone carvings were so detailed that photographers wanted to record them.
How many carved figures can you find?
Kadikoi, from the Camp of Horse Artillery
Roger Fenton photographed the Crimean War camps around the village of Kadikoi. He could not photograph fighting, but his pictures showed people at home where soldiers lived.
What would you pack for a camp like this?
The Ordnance Wharf, Balaklava
Roger Fenton photographed a busy wharf in the harbor of Balaklava, where ships brought guns and supplies for the army. The crowd of ships and crates shows how big the war effort was.
What are the ships carrying?
L'Entente Cordiale
Fenton photographed British and French soldiers together in the Crimea. The title means a friendly understanding, because the two countries fought on the same side.
What kind of friendship does the picture suggest?
Convivial Party, 4th Dragoon Guards
British and French officers share a meal at a camp in Crimea. Fenton's pictures show a friendly side of war that newspapers wanted to see.
What do you think they talked about?
General Sir Henry Barnard
Roger Fenton photographed this British general during the Crimean War. Barnard was the chief of staff to the army and died soon after.
What do you see in the way he stands?
Alexandre Dumas
Nadar photographed his friend Alexandre Dumas, who wrote The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo. Nadar's portraits caught the personality of writers and artists.
What do you think a famous storyteller looks like?
Servants at Rhagatt, Corwen
An amateur photographer, John Lloyd, photographed an older and a younger servant at a house in Wales. The picture shows two people who worked in a big house, side by side.
How are the two different in age and in clothing?
Church at Auvers
Baldus photographed the old church at Auvers in France. Thirty years later, Vincent van Gogh would paint the same church in a famous painting.
Have you seen Van Gogh's church? How is a photograph different from a painting?
Tamil Gateway
This stereograph shows a tall temple gateway, or gopura, in southern India. When you look at the two pictures with a viewer, the gateway seems to stand out in 3D.
How could you make the picture seem 3D without a viewer?
Lord Burghersh
Fenton photographed the young Lord Burghersh during his trip to the Crimea in 1855. He took portraits of the officers and their camps as part of a project for a publisher.
Why would a publisher want pictures from the war?
Louvre, Façade on the Rue de Rivoli
Édouard Baldus photographed the new Louvre façade in Paris in the 1850s. The government hired him to record its great new building projects.
How is a photograph of a building different from the real building?
Study of the Sky
Charles Marville photographed clouds in the sky, a hard thing to catch in the 1850s because the plates saw blue and white as the same. It is a rare early cloud study.
What shapes do you see in the clouds?
Cossack Bay, Balaklava
Fenton photographed the sea at Cossack Bay near Balaklava during the Crimean War. He was one of the first to photograph a war zone, and this view is a quiet moment by the sea.
What does a calm harbor in a war feel like?
The Beach at Sainte-Adresse
Gustave Le Gray photographed the sea from a beach in Normandy. He was trained as a painter, and he found ways to show both the sky and the water in one picture.
How are the sky and the sea different?
The Haloed Sun
Le Gray photographed the sun in the sky with a bright ring around it. To catch such a bright thing was a hard trick in 1856.
Why is it so hard to photograph the sun?
Seascape, Normandy
Le Gray made some of the first beautiful seascapes. He joined two negatives, one for the sea and one for the sky, to get both right.
How do you think he combined two pictures?
The Steamboat
Le Gray photographed a steamboat on the water in the 1850s. A boat moving through the water was a real challenge for early cameras.
How do you think the ship stayed so sharp?
Madame Carrelle
Mayer and Pierson ran a studio in Paris that photographed famous and fashionable people. This portrait of a woman named Madame Carrelle shows a studio style that was copied everywhere.
What do you notice about her dress?
Pavillon Richelieu, Louvre
Baldus photographed the new wing of the Louvre while workers were building it. The government wanted a record of its big project, and the photographs also showed how fine his sharp prints were.
How many windows can you count?
Sculpture at Hoysaleshvara Temple, Halebidu
Richard Oakeley walked 20 days to photograph the carved temple at Halebidu in India. The stone walls are covered in tiny figures and gods, carved nearly 900 years ago.
What kinds of figures can you find in the carvings?
Gioachino Rossini
Nadar photographed the Italian composer Rossini, who wrote the opera The Barber of Seville. Rossini finished 39 operas before he turned 39 and then mostly stopped.
What would you do if you finished a big job at 39?
The Breaking Wave
Gustave Le Gray photographed a big wave breaking on the shore. The foam stands out sharp against the dark water, which was a feat for slow cameras.
How do you think he caught a moving wave?
The Port of Sète
Le Gray photographed the busy port of Sète on the Mediterranean coast of France. He made views of ships and docks that look as if they were painted.
What kinds of ships can you see?
The Mediterranean with Mount Agde
Le Gray photographed the sea and a hill called Mount Agde in southern France. He liked to show the sea and sky as big spaces.
Where does the sea meet the sky?
Artillery Encampment, Camp de Châlons
Le Gray photographed the army camp at Châlons for the French emperor Napoleon III. The camp was for training soldiers, and the photographs recorded the guns and tents.
What do soldiers do at a training camp?
The Great Bull, Tanjore
Linnaeus Tripe photographed the giant stone bull at the temple in Tanjore, India. The bull is Nandi, the mount of the god Shiva, and it is carved from a single block of stone.
How big do you think the bull is compared with the people?
The Miners' Bridge, North Wales
Roger Fenton photographed a wooden bridge over the River Llugwy in Wales. He gave up photography after only 12 years, but his landscapes are still loved.
What would it be like to cross this bridge?
Fallen Statue at the Ramesseum, Thebes
Francis Frith photographed a giant fallen statue of Ramesses II at his temple in Egypt. Frith carried a darkroom on boats and camels, and he often worked in heat so great that the chemicals boiled.
Why would photography chemicals be hard to use in a desert?
Study for Two Ways of Life

Oscar Rejlander made a famous photograph by combining more than 30 negatives. This is a study for it, in which he posed models. It was shocking and clever, and critics argued about whether it was art.
How do you think he combined so many pictures?
There He Goes
Rejlander staged photographs of children and models with careful expressions. He used the camera like a stage, and some of his pictures are funny.
What is the story in the picture?
The Small Grotto, Bois de Boulogne
Charles Marville photographed an artificial cave in a Paris park. The grotto was built to look like nature, and Marville's picture makes it look like a magical forest.
What would you find inside a grotto?
The Pyramids of Saqqara
Francis Frith photographed the old step pyramids of Saqqara in Egypt. He was the first photographer in Egypt to use the wet collodion process, and his glass plates were much sharper than paper.
How is a step pyramid different from the famous pyramids at Giza?
Jama Masjid Gate
Felice Beato photographed a gate of the great mosque in Delhi, India, in 1858. He was one of the first photographers to travel across Asia with a camera.
What shapes do you see in the gate?
Lucknow After the Siege
Felice Beato photographed the ruined buildings of Lucknow in India in 1858, after a long siege. His pictures are an early record of a war scene, showing damaged buildings rather than people.
What would the town have looked like before the siege?
Gateway of the Minakshi Temple
Captain Linnaeus Tripe photographed the colorful gateway of a large temple in Madurai, India. These towers, called gopurams, are covered in thousands of painted figures.
How tall do you think the tower is?
